analysis.investment_thesis: Neochem Bio shows genuine business improvement with ROCE of 27.2% and explosive operating profit growth (4→13 Cr in 2 years), but the Magic Formula earnings yield of ~8.6% (EBIT 13 Cr / EV ~151 Cr) falls well below the 12% minimum threshold. You're paying a fair-to-full price for a highly leveraged micro-cap with barely any free cash flow — not the cheap+good combination the formula demands.
key_strengths: ROCE of 27.2% clears the 25%+ excellence bar — operating capital is being deployed effectively
Strong revenue CAGR (~32%): INR 48→84 Cr, with operating income tripling from 4→13 Cr, suggesting genuine operating leverage
Promoter holding at 66.7% with meaningful DII interest (13.2%) signals some institutional validation
key_risks: Earnings yield ~8.6% (EBIT 13 Cr / EV ~151 Cr) fails the Magic Formula 12% minimum — the stock is not cheap enough to justify the risks
Debt burden of INR 36 Cr vs. equity of 20 Cr (D/E ~1.8x); finance costs of 4 Cr consumed ~31% of operating income in FY25
FCF barely turned positive at 1 Cr in FY25 after two years of negative FCF — high earnings quality risk for a reported 8 Cr net profit
red_flags: Other income of 2 Cr represents ~25% of net profit (8 Cr) — strips out to a thinner underlying earnings base
Cumulative FCF over 3 years: -4 + -3 + 1 = -6 Cr despite 3-year cumulative net profit of ~11 Cr — severe cash conversion problem
Micro-cap at INR 117 Cr market cap with INR 36 Cr debt — any business disruption has limited balance sheet cushion
analysis.detailed_analysis:
On the Magic Formula scorecard, Neochem Bio passes on business quality but fails on valuation. ROCE of 27.2% is legitimately good and the trajectory is encouraging — operating margins expanded from ~8% to ~15% in two years. However, the earnings yield of ~8.6% (EBIT 13 Cr against an enterprise value of roughly 151 Cr: 117 Cr market cap + 36 Cr debt) sits well below the 12% floor where the formula begins to find value. At a P/E of 16x on what looks like a cyclically or one-time boosted profit figure, the market is pricing in continued growth without compensating investors for the risk.

The bigger concern from a capital quality standpoint is the persistent gap between reported profits and free cash flow. Three-year cumulative net profit of ~11 Cr against cumulative FCF of -6 Cr means earnings are being absorbed into working capital and capex — typical for rapidly growing specialty chemical manufacturers, but it means the "cheap" earnings on the income statement aren't landing in the bank. With 36 Cr of borrowings and 4 Cr in annual finance costs, this micro-cap has limited margin of safety. The Magic Formula works by buying great businesses at bargain prices; Neochem Bio is improving but is neither cheap enough nor proven enough at this stage.
